interview_metadata.name: William Wood
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Sure, happy to. I was born in 1968 and grew up in Hempstead on Long Island, in a pretty traditional middle-class household. My dad worked at a Grumman aerospace facility doing technical drafting, and my mom did office work for a local school district. I have one older sister, Carol. We weren't fancy people, but Sunday dinners were a thing, Little League was a thing, and you cut the grass on Saturday before you watched the Yankees game. I was the kid who took apart the family VCR to see how it worked and then, miraculously, got it back together. I went to public high school in Hempstead, played baseball, was decent in math, terrible at art, and I got into Stony Brook for undergrad, computer science. That was the late '80s when relational databases were really becoming the thing, and I got hooked on Oracle in an internship the summer before my senior year. Graduated in 1990, took a junior DBA role at a financial services firm in Midtown, and basically have been doing some version of that work ever since. I met my wife, Linda, at a friend's wedding in '94 — she's a high school English teacher. We got married in 1996, bought our place in Little Neck in 2001, and have two kids: Daniel, who's 27 and lives in Brooklyn working in product, and Emily, who's 24 and finishing a master's in public health at Columbia. Along the way I got my master's at NYU part-time in the early 2000s, switched companies a few times — I'm at a midsize health insurance carrier now leading their database team. The big milestones outside of family were probably 9/11, which I lived through working a few blocks from the towers, and my dad passing in 2014. Otherwise it's been a pretty steady arc — work hard, raise kids, keep showing up.

follow_ups.question: You mentioned getting hooked on Oracle that summer — what was it about it that pulled you in?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, it was the feeling that I could finally see the rules behind something invisible. I was writing SQL queries against a customer database and you could literally watch the data tell you a story — who bought what, when, how often. It was like solving a puzzle where the puzzle also paid you. I had a mentor named Frank Russo at that internship who'd sit with me at the end of the day and walk through execution plans, and that stuck with me for life.

follow_ups.question: You mentioned 9/11 — what was that day like for you?
follow_ups.response: I was at 75 Wall Street, about four blocks south. I remember the second plane more than the first because by then we all knew. We walked north up the FDR with thousands of other people. I couldn't reach Linda for about three hours. Daniel was two years old. I still don't love loud planes overhead, even now.

follow_ups.question: How did losing your dad in 2014 shift things for you?
follow_ups.response: It made me a less patient man about wasted time, and a more patient man about everything else. He was 71, pancreatic cancer, very fast. After that I started actually taking my vacation days, and I started cooking more — he was the one who taught me how to grill a lamb chop properly.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, around 2008 I had a real fork. I was being recruited by a tech consultancy out of Boston — big bump in pay, a lot of travel, very much the 'become a road warrior' path. At the same time my current employer offered me a quieter team-lead role with a tuition reimbursement so I could finish my master's. Linda was teaching, Daniel was 9, Emily was 6, and we'd just refinanced the house. I sat with it for about a month. In the end I took the team-lead role and stayed home. I think if I'd taken the consulting job I'd probably be making considerably more money and I'd also probably be divorced. So that decision sort of set the whole shape of the next fifteen years — I went deep on architecture instead of going wide on travel, and I got to actually be at my kids' games.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever second-guess that choice?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, almost never. Maybe once when I see a college classmate's LinkedIn and they're a partner somewhere. But then I remember I coached Daniel's Little League team for four years and I'm at peace.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: That one was a conscious choice. I actually made a pros-and-cons spreadsheet, which I know is a very DBA thing to do. Linda and I sat down at the kitchen table on a Sunday and worked through it together.

follow_ups.question: Was Linda's input the deciding factor?
follow_ups.response: She didn't push me one way, but she said something like, 'whichever you choose, I want to be married to the version of you that comes out of it.' That kind of made the answer obvious.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Frank Russo, that old mentor I mentioned, gave me about an hour on the phone and it helped a lot. I don't think any organization could have done much — these are pretty personal calls. Having someone older who'd already walked the path was worth more than any career-coaching service.

follow_ups.question: Do you try to be that person for younger DBAs now?
follow_ups.response: I try. I run an informal mentoring group at work — three or four junior folks I meet with monthly. I tell them: ask me the awkward questions you can't ask your manager.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: Yes — Linda, my wife of almost 30 years, and our two kids Daniel and Emily. Linda teaches sophomore English at a public high school in Bayside; she's been at the same school for 22 years. She's the warmer one of the two of us, definitely the one who remembers everyone's birthdays. Daniel is 27, works as a product manager at a fintech startup in Brooklyn, lives in Park Slope with his girlfriend Mara. He's the more cautious one — he runs through risks the way I do. Emily is 24, finishing her MPH at Columbia, focused on health equity. She's the loud one in the family in the best way, organizes everything. We do Sunday dinner pretty much every other week — they take the train out or we go in. My sister Carol lives in Garden City with her husband Tom; we see them maybe once a month. My mom is 84, still in the house I grew up in in Hempstead — I drive out there every other Saturday to do whatever needs doing, change a smoke detector battery, take her to brunch.

follow_ups.question: What does Sunday dinner usually look like?
follow_ups.response: Linda sets the table around 6, I cook — usually something slow like a braise or a roast. Right now I'm on a lamb shoulder kick. Glass of Sangiovese, the kids argue about politics, Linda referees. We try to keep phones off the table.

follow_ups.question: How's your mom doing these days?
follow_ups.response: Physically pretty good — she walks a mile every morning. Cognitively she's starting to repeat herself a bit. Carol and I have started talking about whether we need to think about an aide a few hours a week.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: Just my brother-in-law Tom and my niece Sarah and nephew Jake on Carol's side. I'm closer to Sarah — she's a graphic designer in Manhattan and we grab lunch a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Sarah usually talk about?
follow_ups.response: Career stuff, mostly. She's figuring out whether to freelance full-time. I give her the boring financial-planning version of advice and she rolls her eyes appropriately.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Definitely. My closest friend is Mike Pellegrino — we've known each other since Stony Brook, he's a cardiologist out in Manhasset. We have a standing Tuesday phone call on my drive home, and we go fly-fishing in the Catskills two weekends a year. There's also my baseball crew — about eight guys from the Little Neck league I see every Sunday morning in season. And the tech meetup folks; there's a NYC SQL Server user group I help organize, maybe twenty regulars I see monthly. Linda and I also have couple friends — the Garcias and the Cohens — we do dinner with them every month or so.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Mike talk about on those Tuesday calls?
follow_ups.response: Honestly half of it is the Yankees. The other half is the actual stuff — kids, parents getting older, work frustrations. He's the person I tell when I'm worried about something I won't tell Linda yet.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We're in Little Neck, which is the far northeast corner of Queens, right up against the Nassau County line. It's quiet — feels more suburban than city. Tree-lined streets, mostly single-family homes from the '40s through the '60s. Demographically it's really mixed: a lot of Korean and Chinese families have moved in over the last 20 years, alongside the older Italian, Irish, and Jewish families that have been here forever. Northern Boulevard has all the restaurants — there's a Korean place called Cho Dang Gol I go to once a week, a great bagel spot on the corner of Little Neck Parkway. The LIRR station is a five-minute walk from our house, which is why we bought there — I can be in Penn in 35 minutes. Alley Pond Park is right next door, which is where I hike and run.

follow_ups.question: How has the neighborhood changed since you moved in 2001?
follow_ups.response: A lot more diverse, and the housing prices have gone way up. Our house was $385K in 2001; comps now are pushing $1.1 million. The downside is younger families have a harder time getting in.

follow_ups.question: What's your relationship with your immediate neighbors like?
follow_ups.response: Friendly. Mr. Chen next door and I trade vegetables from our gardens in the summer. We do a block barbecue every June. Nobody's in each other's business but everyone would notice if a stranger was on the block.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very safe. I walk the dog at 10pm without thinking about it. There was a car break-in down the block about a year ago and it was the talk of the block for two weeks, which tells you something.

follow_ups.question: Has that always been true or has it shifted?
follow_ups.response: Pretty consistent over 25 years. Maybe a little quieter now than in the early 2000s, actually.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The ups are space, quiet, good schools, an actual yard, and the train. The downs are property taxes — we pay around $14,000 a year — and the fact that for a single-malt scotch or a late-night anything you really have to go into the city. But we're old enough now that we mostly don't want to.

follow_ups.question: Have those taxes ever made you think about leaving?
follow_ups.response: We've kicked around the idea of downsizing once Emily's truly out, maybe Hudson Valley or Connecticut. But not seriously. The roots are deep here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it's me, Linda, and our dog Otis — he's a 7-year-old chocolate lab. Emily technically still has a room here and stays over maybe one weekend a month, but her real address is her apartment in Morningside Heights. Daniel's fully out. So functionally it's a two-person household plus the dog.

follow_ups.question: How was the adjustment when Emily moved out?
follow_ups.response: Quieter than I expected, in both senses. The first month Linda and I sort of looked at each other like, 'so… what do we do now?' We figured it out. We started doing date night Fridays again.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone permanent. Linda, me, and the dog.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Emily about once a month, and Daniel and Mara come for dinner and occasionally stay over on a holiday.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, no one in that category.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays are pretty regimented. I'm up at 5:45, coffee, walk Otis for 20 minutes, on the LIRR at 7:08, at my desk in Midtown by 8. I work through about 6, take the 6:18 home, and I'm at the kitchen counter by 7:15. Linda and I eat around 7:45. Three evenings a week I'm reading or watching something with her; Tuesdays I have the call with Mike; Wednesdays we go to a 7pm spin class together at the Y. Saturdays in spring and summer are baseball mornings followed by errands and cooking. Sundays are family dinner or visiting my mom. Once a month I'm out at a jazz show or a tech meetup on a Thursday.

follow_ups.question: Is there a part of that week you look forward to most?
follow_ups.response: Saturday morning baseball, no contest. The smell of the field, the guys, a bad coffee from the deli. It resets me.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: 10:30 on a school night, 11:30 on a Saturday. Linda's an earlier bird — she's out by 10.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I'm a senior database architect at a midsize health insurance company headquartered in Manhattan. I lead a team of seven DBAs. Day-to-day I split between architecture design — we're in the middle of a big migration from on-prem SQL Server to Azure SQL — production troubleshooting when something hits the fan, and a lot of meetings with engineering leads and the compliance team because of HIPAA. I work Monday through Friday roughly 8 to 6, but I'm on call one week a month and that can mean a 3am page. I do almost no work on weekends unless something is genuinely on fire.

follow_ups.question: How often does the 3am page actually happen?
follow_ups.response: On a bad on-call week, twice. On a good week, zero. The migration has made it worse this year — we're running hybrid right now, and hybrid means twice the surface area.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: Yeah, a few. Saturday mornings I visit my mom every other week, which we already touched on. Once a month Linda and I volunteer at the Little Neck branch of the Queens Library running a tech-literacy session for seniors — basics like how to spot a phishing email, how to use FaceTime with their grandkids. I'm also the unofficial IT support for my mom and for two of my older neighbors. I pay the household bills — Linda handles taxes, I handle monthly cash flow.

follow_ups.question: What's the most common question you get at the senior tech session?
follow_ups.response: 'My iPad is asking me to update and I'm scared to press the button.' I'd say a third of the questions are some flavor of that. The other big one is scam texts — they get a fake Chase fraud alert and we walk through how to verify.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Two things. One, the company moved to hybrid in early 2024, so I'm in the office Tuesday through Thursday and remote Monday and Friday. That's been a net positive — I get those morning dog walks longer on remote days. Two, Linda and I started the Wednesday spin class about four months ago because my doctor pushed me on my cholesterol. I'm not loving it but I'm doing it.

follow_ups.question: Has the hybrid setup changed how the team works?
follow_ups.response: We had to be intentional. We do a 9:30 standup every weekday on Teams, and we try to put hard collaboration meetings on Wednesdays when everyone's in. The juniors still need in-person time — that's where most of the learning happens.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Both my kids are adults now, so they're not in school in that sense. But back when they were in high school it was pretty classic — school 8 to 3, Daniel had baseball or robotics after, Emily had debate team and student government, dinner together by 7 on the nights we could make it work, then homework till 10 or 11. Linda was the homework supervisor; I was the 'did you read the news today' guy. Saturdays were sports and music — Emily took piano for nine years.

follow_ups.question: Did either of them end up keeping up the piano or sports?
follow_ups.response: Emily still plays piano when she's home, mostly for stress relief. Daniel hasn't picked up a baseball bat in five years and it kills me a little.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Pretty minimal. I've been pulled over twice in 35 years of driving — once for a busted taillight in maybe 2009, once for speeding on the LIE around 2017. Both times, polite cop, warning, no ticket. The 105th Precinct covers our neighborhood and they've been at our block party. That's about the extent of it.

follow_ups.question: Did you grow up trusting the police?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I did. My uncle on my mom's side was Nassau County PD. So it was always sort of a respected thing in our house growing up.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Honestly nothing dramatic. The car break-in I mentioned — I filed a report online, an officer came by the next morning to take a statement, nothing came of it. Standard stuff.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No one in my immediate or extended family has been arrested, as far as I know. I had a college roommate who got a DUI senior year, that's the closest I've been to it.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in every general — presidential, midterm, mayoral. I'm less consistent on primaries, I'll admit. New York is a closed primary state and I'm registered Democrat, so I do try to show up for those when I remember. Linda's better about it than I am — she's the one who reminds me about school board elections.

follow_ups.question: How do you usually decide on local races?
follow_ups.response: I read the Queens Daily Eagle and the local City Council newsletters. For judges I'll be honest, I sometimes vote the bar association recommendations because I just can't research everyone.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd call myself center-left, pragmatic. Socially liberal — I'm very pro-choice, pro-gay-marriage, pro-immigration, pro-gun-control. Fiscally I'm more moderate; I want a working safety net and serious infrastructure spending, but I also work in healthcare and I see how complicated cost containment actually is. I think a lot about HIPAA and patient data and the right tradeoffs there. I voted Obama twice, Clinton in 2016, Biden in 2020, and Harris in 2024. I'm a Democrat but I have real frustrations with the party — I think the left wing has gotten a little allergic to people like me who think incrementalism actually moves the ball. I have a few college friends who've gone hard right over the last decade and we just don't talk about it anymore, which is sad. On the local level I tend to support whichever candidate seems serious about transit, schools, and not letting the city's quality of life slide. I worry a lot about polarization and I worry a lot about what AI is going to do to a chunk of the workforce in the next ten years.

follow_ups.question: What's an issue where your view doesn't fit neatly into either party?
follow_ups.response: Immigration enforcement, maybe. I'm pro-immigration overall — Queens runs on immigrant labor and immigrant talent — but I also think a country has to be able to know who's coming in. I think Democrats sometimes flinch from saying that out loud.

follow_ups.question: Has working in healthcare changed your political views?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I went in as a 'single-payer would fix everything' guy in my 30s. Twenty years in, I'm more like, 'something closer to a public option, plus aggressive price regulation on drugs and hospitals, is what's actually achievable.' The system is way more tangled than I thought.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: In the last couple of years I've gotten more worried about institutional damage — courts, civil service, election administration — and that's pushed me to care more about boring procedural stuff than I used to. I've also gotten more skeptical of social-media-driven politics on both sides. After the 2024 election I deliberately cut my Twitter use way down and started subscribing to a couple of long-form newsletters instead. I haven't changed parties, but I've become a 'lower the temperature' Democrat more than a 'fight every fight' Democrat.

follow_ups.question: Which newsletters do you read now?
follow_ups.response: Slow Boring, The Dispatch for the conservative-but-sane view, and Ezra Klein's podcast. Plus the Times daily.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat to a lot, depending on the moment. 2020 hit me hard — the George Floyd video was something I watched once and I'll never need to watch again. Linda and I had real conversations with Daniel and Emily that summer, and I had some conversations with my mom that didn't go as well as I'd hoped. At work we did some unconscious-bias training that I thought was mostly well-intentioned but uneven. I'd say the movement made me more aware of how much I'd absorbed without examining it, and also more aware of how few Black colleagues I've had in 30 years in databases, which is its own conversation about the pipeline.

follow_ups.question: What did your mom's reaction look like?
follow_ups.response: She's of a generation where 'I don't see color' was meant as a virtue, and explaining why that framing has limits to an 82-year-old in 2020 was a bridge too far. We agreed to disagree.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core point — that there's a real pattern of disparate policing outcomes and that it deserves systemic attention — is just true. Where I get more cautious is on specific policy proposals; 'defund' as a slogan I think did the movement a lot of damage in places like Queens where people across races actually want a functioning police presence. I'm more in the 'reform, train, accountability, alternative-response for mental health calls' camp. I've watched the data on traffic stops in particular and it's pretty undeniable.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we made real progress over my lifetime and we also have a long way to go. Queens is the most diverse county in the country and on most days it works — kids of every background go to the same schools, eat at the same restaurants, play on the same baseball teams. But I'm also aware that economic gaps haven't closed nearly as much as social ones, and the recent rollback of DEI programs across corporate America bothers me. I think when companies retreat from those programs it sends a signal that lands harder than the programs themselves ever did.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I haven't been to a protest. I've talked about it with family and close friends, donated to the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and to a local Queens youth nonprofit. At work I pushed to keep mentorship programs running when budget pressure was on. Quiet work, not loud work, is honestly my temperament.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Mixed. Mike, my doctor friend, is very engaged — he sits on the board of a community clinic in the Bronx. Linda's school has done a lot of curricular work on this and she's been involved. The baseball guys are all over the map politically and we mostly don't get into it on Sundays. Some of my older relatives are tuned out or hostile.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Pretty good for 57, with a couple of asterisks. I'm 5'10", 198 pounds, which is about 15 pounds heavier than my doctor would like. My blood pressure has crept up — I'm on 10mg of lisinopril daily as of last year. My LDL cholesterol is elevated, that's the spin class motivation. I had arthroscopic knee surgery on my right meniscus in 2019, baseball-related, and it's fine now but it tells me when it's going to rain. Otherwise no major chronic conditions, no diabetes, vision is correctable, hearing is fine.

follow_ups.question: Who's your primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Dr. Patel out of NYU Langone in Garden City. I've been with him about 12 years. Linda's at the same practice.

follow_ups.question: Are you on any other medications besides the lisinopril?
follow_ups.response: A daily multivitamin and vitamin D in the winter. That's it for now. My doctor's been hinting about a statin but we're trying lifestyle first.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: Linda cooks healthy by default, we have a park next door, I have a baseball league that gets me moving, and I have decent insurance. Hard: a desk job, on-call weeks that wreck my sleep, business dinners where wine flows freely, and the fact that I genuinely like cooking rich food on weekends. The cooking is the real Achilles heel.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Last year, in early 2025, I had a scare — I was having intermittent chest tightness during a Saturday game. Dr. Patel sent me for a stress test and a CT angiogram. The results came back clean — no significant blockages — but that's when the hypertension diagnosis came in and the lisinopril started. It was a wake-up call. I also had a colonoscopy in late 2024, on schedule, all normal. Otherwise no broken bones, no surgeries since 2019.

follow_ups.question: How did the chest tightness feel in the moment?
follow_ups.response: Honestly more annoying than scary the first couple of times. The third time I felt it I stopped running between bases and that's when I called the doctor on Monday. Linda made me go.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Not significantly. The knee surgery in 2019 had me on a desk for six weeks but I could work fine. The chest scare cost me maybe a week of evening focus while I was waiting on tests. Nothing has materially affected my ability to do my job or be present for my family.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes — my dad's cancer in 2014 was the big one. He was diagnosed in March and we lost him in August, very fast. I took two weeks off work at the end. More recently, my mom's slowly-creeping cognitive decline is on my radar, and Linda's mother in Florida had a heart procedure in 2023 that meant a couple of trips down. So nothing acute right now, but it's the slow-motion stuff that comes with being in your late 50s.

follow_ups.question: How are you handling the worry about your mom?
follow_ups.response: Mostly by doing — the every-other-Saturday visits, getting her enrolled in a meal delivery service, putting cameras at her front door. Action calms me down more than talking does.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We've been really fortunate. My employer's plan is generous — it's PPO with a reasonable deductible, and most of our doctors are in network. The biggest pain point is just scheduling — getting a specialist appointment in Manhattan can take three months. We've never had to forgo care. Linda's dental work last year wasn't fully covered and we just paid out of pocket. I'm aware that's a privileged position to be in.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Linda does acupuncture for migraine prevention and swears by it — she's been seeing a practitioner in Bayside for about ten years. I'm a skeptic but I can't argue with her results. Emily got into meditation and yoga in college and that's a real part of her routine. I'll do the occasional Epsom salt bath after a bad knee day but that's about as woo as I get.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I don't smoke and never really did beyond a cigar at a wedding. I drink wine pretty regularly — probably three or four glasses a week on a normal week, more around the holidays or when I'm cooking on a Saturday. I wouldn't call it coping per se, it's more of a pleasure. During my dad's illness in 2014 I definitely poured a bigger glass at night, and I noticed and pulled back when things settled.

follow_ups.question: Has the doctor said anything about the wine?
follow_ups.response: He said three or four glasses a week is fine, more than seven is not. So I try to stay on the right side of that ledger.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: Nothing like that. I had Percocet briefly after the knee surgery in 2019 and stopped as soon as Tylenol could do the job — maybe four days total. I've never used marijuana, even now that it's legal in New York. It's not a moral thing, it's just not my thing.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Through my employer plan. Premium comes out of my paycheck, deductible is $1,500 for the family, out-of-pocket max around $6,000. We hit the deductible most years between routine stuff and one of us having something. We have an HSA we contribute to and I treat it as a second retirement account — invest it and don't touch it.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Strongly pro-vaccine. Full COVID series including the most recent updated booster, annual flu shot, got the shingles vaccine when I turned 50, will get the new RSV one when my doctor says it's time. I work in healthcare and the data is what it is.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Dr. Patel first. Then CDC and NIH publications. I've read a lot of Katelyn Jetelina's Your Local Epidemiologist newsletter since COVID. And I'll cross-check with the NEJM if it's something I'm really digging into. I don't take medical info from social media.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mostly steady, with some undercurrents. Professionally I'm in a good phase — the migration project is going well and I feel respected. Personally there's a quiet weight: my mom's slow decline, the chest scare, and the realization that I'm legitimately closer to retirement than to the start of my career. Linda and I are in a really good place. I'm thinking a lot about what the next ten years look like — do I push for the CDO-track move, or do I optimize for time with people I love. Not anxious about it, exactly, but it's there.

follow_ups.question: How does that 'quiet weight' show up day to day?
follow_ups.response: Mostly in moments — a song my dad liked comes on, or my mom calls me Carol's name by accident on the phone. I don't dwell, but I notice.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: The week between the chest tightness and the clean stress-test results last spring was rough. I'm normally a pretty grounded guy, but I caught myself running through worst-case scenarios — would Linda be okay financially, was the will updated, had I told Daniel the things I wanted to tell him. I didn't sleep great. I talked to Linda about it on a Friday night and that helped. The results came back the following Tuesday and I felt like I exhaled for the first time in nine days.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not diagnosed with anything. I'd say I have a normal baseline of low-grade work anxiety, especially on-call weeks. After my dad died in 2014 I went through what I'd call a six-month low — not clinical depression, but a heaviness — and I did six sessions with a therapist that fall and that was enough to get me back on the rails. Haven't been since.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Linda's pretty resilient — teaching is high stress but she's good at compartmentalizing. Emily had a tough sophomore year of college, did some therapy and meds for anxiety, and she's in a good place now. Daniel runs hot — gets stressed at work, decompresses by running long miles. Nobody in crisis.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Not particularly. I was raised Methodist — my parents took us to a church in Hempstead till I was about 13, then it sort of faded. Linda was raised Catholic, similar pattern. We got married in a church to please her parents and we baptized both kids. We do Christmas Eve at a local Episcopal church because we like the music, and that's about the extent of organized religion in our lives. I'd describe myself as spiritually curious but not affiliated — I find more of that feeling on a hike in Alley Pond at dawn than in a pew. I respect people who have a strong faith and I think the community piece of it is genuinely valuable; I just don't have it.

follow_ups.question: Do the kids identify with anything?
follow_ups.response: Emily would say agnostic. Daniel would say atheist with a soft spot for Buddhist meditation.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I'm a light user. I have a Facebook account I check maybe twice a week, mostly to see the baseball league posts and family stuff from cousins. LinkedIn I'm on daily — it's basically a professional necessity in my field, and I post occasionally about database trends. Instagram I have but I lurk; I'll post a Cinque Terre vacation photo or a plate of food maybe once a quarter. I deleted Twitter/X off my phone after the 2024 election — I still have the account, I just don't open it. I don't do TikTok at all. Linda's similar.

follow_ups.question: What kinds of posts do you put on LinkedIn?
follow_ups.response: Mostly reposts of articles about cloud database migrations or AI integration with annotations. Occasionally a 'here's what I learned at this conference' post. Nothing personal.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: No, that's not where I'd go. I'd call Mike, or talk to Linda, or sit with it. Social media for emotional support feels like the wrong tool to me — like trying to fix a leaky pipe with a stapler.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress is moderately up because of the migration project and the on-call rotation. I've added the spin class on Wednesdays and I've been more disciplined about taking lunch walks. Cutting Twitter has measurably helped my mood. That's been the biggest delta in the last six months.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: Just Linda and the dog Otis.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Linda and I share it — joint accounts.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Mortgage is the biggest at about $3,200 a month, then property taxes which we escrow, groceries around $1,000, utilities and internet about $400, car costs for two cars around $700 all in, and we sent Emily $600 to help with rent.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: Last month was roughly $9,500. That's a little high for a normal month — we had a vet bill for Otis and Linda's car needed brakes. A typical month is closer to $8,500. The variable buckets are restaurants, travel, and home maintenance.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own. We've been in this house since 2001 — refinanced twice, currently on a 15-year fixed at 2.875% that we locked in during the pandemic. Should be paid off in about seven years.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Winter heating spikes the utility bill — January and February were both over $500. Summer air conditioning is a smaller spike. November and December are heavy on gifts and travel — we did a big family Thanksgiving and a holiday trip to see Linda's mom in Florida. Spring brings the property tax payments, which is always a bracing reminder. Late August was Emily's tuition wire for fall semester.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: Out of cash flow, mostly. We keep a sinking fund for big known expenses like property tax and tuition, and a separate emergency fund. We haven't had to dip into the emergency fund in a few years.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We save aggressively. I max my 401(k) including catch-up contributions — that's $30,500 a year right now — Linda contributes to a 403(b) through the school district, we both have IRAs, we have a taxable brokerage account with Vanguard, the HSA, and a high-yield savings account at Marcus for the emergency fund. We probably save around 22% of gross income. That's the inheritance from my dad — he was big on 'pay yourself first.'

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Retirement is the big target. I'd like to be able to step back from full-time work around 63 or 64, do some consulting on the side. Beyond that we save for travel — we're planning a Greek Islands sailing trip for our 30th anniversary in 2026 — and we have a small fund we'd like to help the kids with for down payments eventually.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: Just the mortgage. No car loans — we pay cash for cars and drive them ten years. No credit card debt — we pay off in full every month. My grad school loans are long gone. We helped Emily with most of her undergrad so she has minimal loans, and we're paying her grad tuition out of pocket.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: Honestly, that hasn't happened. I'm aware that's a real privilege. The closest we get is making a conscious choice to postpone something — we delayed redoing the kitchen this year because the contractor estimates came in higher than we wanted.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Senior Database Architect. My core duties are designing the data architecture for our claims, member, and provider systems — that means deciding what runs on SQL Server, what runs on Postgres, what goes in MongoDB, what lives in the data lake on Azure. I lead a team of seven, including two senior DBAs and five mid-to-junior folks. I do the high-availability and disaster recovery planning, I write the change-management standards, I review schema changes for the engineering teams. I'm the technical point person on our HIPAA compliance audits. I do performance tuning when an escalation hits — query plans, indexing strategy. And I spend a lot of time in cross-functional planning meetings making the case for or against architectural decisions to product managers and execs.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No. I'm a salaried exempt employee, not unionized. Linda's the union member in the family — UFT.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: All 52 weeks if you count paid time off. I took three weeks of vacation and a few scattered sick days.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: About 50 hours in a normal week, more like 60 on an on-call week.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: Yes, full week.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: No, just the one. I occasionally guest lecture in a NYU SPS data management course but that's barely paid — it's more for the love of it.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: One main job. One guest lecture last month at NYU, paid a nominal honorarium.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: Gross pay last month was about $16,500. Net after taxes, 401(k), and health premium is around $9,200 in my checking.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Bi-weekly, every other Friday. Plus an annual bonus in March.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Combined we brought in about $24,000 gross last month. Linda's teacher salary plus her summer curriculum work is in there. Our combined annual is somewhere around $295,000 before bonus.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, jointly with Linda. We use a CPA in Bayside, Mr. Nakamura, who's done our taxes for fifteen years. We always itemize because of property taxes and mortgage interest.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: Nine years at this company. Benefits are strong — full PPO health, dental, vision, four weeks PTO, a separate week of sick, 401(k) with 6% match, generous parental leave I don't use anymore, HSA option, ESPP, tuition reimbursement, and a $1,500 annual learning budget.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: Good across the board. My VP, Susan Park, has been my boss for four years and we work really well — she trusts me to run my domain. The team likes each other; we do a monthly team lunch and an annual offsite. I'm closer with my senior DBAs than my juniors just by virtue of more shared history.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Mostly predictable except for on-call. I set my own hours within reason — if I need to step out for a doctor's appointment or be at Emily's graduation, nobody bats an eye. The flexibility is real and I value it. The unpredictability is the on-call week, which is one week a month and can blow up a Tuesday night.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not an issue anymore — kids are adults. When they were little Linda's schedule as a teacher matched their school schedule and we managed without daycare for the most part.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No, none of those.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: Income has been steady. The only month that looked lighter was March because the annual bonus skews timing and my deductions front-load early in the year. Nothing where I'd say we were stretched.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: Yes, easily out of checking. We keep a six-month emergency fund in Marcus on top of that. $400 wouldn't move the needle.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Grateful and reasonably confident. We're on track for the retirement I want around 64. The house will be paid off before then. The kids are launched or close to it. The risks I worry about are healthcare costs in retirement, the possibility of a long-term care situation for my mom or eventually for us, and big economic shocks that could hit the brokerage. I don't lose sleep over money the way some people I know do, and I try not to take that for granted. I came from a household where my parents talked about bills at the kitchen table, so I'm always a little vigilant.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: Married. Linda and I have been married since June 1996 — we'll hit 30 years next year.

transcript.question_text: For our records, we also need your date of birth. Could you please provide that?
transcript.response: October 14, 1968.

transcript.question_text: Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Yes, born in the U.S.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Hempstead, New York. Mineola Hospital, technically.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: White — Anglo-American, English and Scotch-Irish ancestry on both sides.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: Master's degree — MS in Information Systems from NYU, 2005.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: Not formally. I'm working on an AWS Data Analytics certification but that's self-study.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No, never served.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Raised Methodist, currently unaffiliated. If pressed I'd write 'none' or 'spiritual but not religious.'

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: Democrat. Moderately strongly — I've voted Democratic in every presidential since 1992 and I'm registered Democrat. I wouldn't call myself a die-hard partisan; I have real disagreements with the left flank of the party and I respect plenty of moderate Republicans I've worked with over the years. But on the major issues — choice, climate, healthcare, civil rights, the rule of law — I'm pretty consistently with the Democrats.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Democratic Party, clearly.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Hempstead, New York. Same house I grew up in, where my mom still lives.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, both biological parents, my whole childhood.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My older sister Carol — she's three years older than me — and a series of dogs. No other relatives in the house.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: Associate's degree from Nassau Community College in drafting technology.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: High school diploma. She started college part-time when I was in middle school but never finished.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, from the time I was about 8 onward.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She was an administrative assistant in the central office of the Hempstead school district. She handled payroll paperwork, scheduling for the superintendent, parent communications, and a lot of the day-to-day office management. She worked there for about 25 years.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: A public school district — the Hempstead Union Free School District, central administration building. Public sector, K-12 education.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my entire childhood.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: He was a technical draftsman at Grumman Aerospace. He drew the engineering schematics for aircraft components — by hand early in his career, then on CAD systems by the mid-'80s. He took a lot of pride in precision. He worked at Grumman until they downsized in the early '90s, then bounced through a couple of smaller defense contractors.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: Grumman Aerospace Corporation, a major defense contractor on Long Island that made military aircraft — F-14 Tomcats, the Lunar Module, things like that. After Grumman it was smaller aerospace and defense sub-contractors doing similar drafting work.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: I hope Linda and I are still together, healthy, and traveling more — the Greek Islands trip, eventually a proper trip to Japan beyond just Kyoto, maybe a few months in Italy. I hope I've made the move into a Chief Data Officer or Data Architecture Lead role and that I've built a team and a mentorship program I'm genuinely proud of, and then I hope I've stepped back from full-time work around 64 to do consulting and teaching. I hope both kids are settled — not necessarily married with kids, just rooted in lives they chose. I hope my mom has a peaceful next chapter. I hope I'm still playing baseball, even if it's slower. I hope the country is in a less anxious place than it is right now.

follow_ups.question: What's the one thing you'd most like to have done by 65 that you haven't done yet?
follow_ups.response: Published a real book, or at least a long-form set of essays, on data architecture done well. Something my younger colleagues might keep on their shelf.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Linda and the kids, first and without qualification. After that: integrity in the work, the friendships that have lasted, and the small everyday rituals — the coffee at 5:45, the Saturday game, the Sunday dinner. I've come to believe the durable stuff is the small stuff, repeated.

summaries.demographer: William Wood is a 57-year-old white, non-Hispanic, U.S.-born married male (Q84-Q89) living in Little Neck, Queens with his wife Linda and their dog, in a household with no minor children and a mortgaged single-family home owned since 2001 (Q11, Q58). He holds a graduate degree (MS Information Systems, NYU 2005) and earns a high six-figure salary as a Senior Database Architect, with a combined household income near $295K (Q72, Q74, Q90). He is a second-generation educated professional whose father had an associate's in drafting at Grumman and mother an HS diploma working in school-district administration (Q100-Q107), and he tracks the classic late-career trajectory of an empty-nester with college-educated adult children, aging widowed-or-soon-to-be parent, and active retirement planning (Q05, Q62, Q83).
summaries.behavioral_economist: William displays the textbook profile of a high-savings, low-debt, planning-oriented household: ~22% gross savings rate, maxed 401(k) with catch-up, HSA-as-second-retirement, six-month emergency fund, no consumer debt, and a deliberate 'pay yourself first' frame inherited from his father (Q60-Q63, Q82). His major life choices have favored long-horizon optionality and time with family over short-term income — turning down a high-paying Boston consulting role in 2008 for team-lead with tuition reimbursement, and using a pros-and-cons spreadsheet to make it (Q02, Q03). He is loss-averse on existential risks (retirement healthcare, long-term care, market shocks) but comfortable with everyday spending and discretionary splurges on tech, jazz, and travel; peer influence is filtered through trusted experts (Dr. Patel, CPA, mentor) rather than crowds, and he has actively pruned attention-economy inputs by deleting X (Q25, Q48, Q50, Q83).
summaries.political_scientist: William is a consistently voting, moderately strong, registered Democrat who has supported every Democratic presidential nominee since 1992 and identifies as center-left and pragmatic, socially liberal and fiscally moderate (Q23, Q24, Q95, Q96). His civic engagement is dense but low-visibility: monthly senior tech-literacy volunteering at Queens Library, neighborhood block barbecues, donations to the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and a Queens youth nonprofit, organizing a SQL Server user group, and reading the Queens Daily Eagle for local elections (Q07, Q17, Q23, Q29). He shows high institutional trust (police, doctors, CDC, courts), worries about institutional erosion and polarization, and has explicitly shifted toward 'lower the temperature' politics by trading Twitter for long-form newsletters (Slow Boring, The Dispatch, Ezra Klein) after 2024 (Q25, Q42, Q48).
summaries.psychologist: William presents as a high-conscientiousness, emotionally stable, and securely attached individual whose identity is anchored in being a steady provider, mentor, husband, and father — values he repeatedly invokes through 'small stuff repeated' rituals (5:45 coffee, Saturday baseball, Sunday dinner) (Q15, Q109). He copes through action and structured social outlets (calling Mike, talking to Linda, exercise, mentorship) rather than substances or rumination, and has only one self-reported clinical contact — six therapy sessions after his father's death in 2014 — with no current diagnoses, though a 2025 cardiac scare produced a brief, well-articulated anticipatory anxiety episode (Q38, Q39, Q44, Q45). His cognitive style is analytical and risk-aware (literal spreadsheet for life choices, execution-plan thinking), but tempered by relational warmth and meaning-making around mortality, his father's death, and his mother's decline (Q01, Q02, Q35, Q43). Motivationally he balances generativity (mentorship, library volunteering, future CDO move) against a clear time-with-loved-ones horizon, planning a phased retirement at 63-64 (Q04, Q62, Q108).
